_what_this_is: The entry gate, answered BEFORE drafting. The threshold question is whether a well-informed non-expert would confidently believe something the primary sources do not support.

belief._note: What the reader already believes, stated as they would state it. If you cannot write this sentence, there is nothing to correct and no subject -- which is how the tobacco-analogy candidate died.
belief.statement: Inclusive education programmes, such as training teachers, making schools accessible, providing assistive devices, and getting communities and parents on board, help children with disabilities in poorer countries attend school and learn. Putting them in mainstream schools with support works better than separate special schools. The main problem is too little funding, not uncertainty about what works.
belief.how_we_know_they_believe_it: The coverage that settled it. Named outlets, quoted headlines. Not 'it is widely assumed'.

what_the_sources_show._note: What the primary sources actually support, and which sources.

direction._note: CORRECTS, CONFIRMS or NARROWS. This field exists so the contrarianism guard can count. A publication whose answer is always CORRECTS is performing scepticism rather than assessing evidence, and is not to be trusted.

reader_with_a_decision: A programme officer at a donor, NGO or education ministry in a low- or middle-income country deciding which disability-inclusive education interventions to fund or scale (teacher training, assistive technology, community-based rehabilitation, cash transfers, accessible infrastructure, resource rooms), and whether to commission rigorous evaluation before scaling.

public_record_check._note: NOT 'has anybody published this'. On any contested question, somebody has. The question is whether it has been carried WHERE THIS READER WOULD FIND IT. Run the counterexample hunter on the belief statement, not on the finding.
public_record_check.our_contribution: translation, extension, or correction of the prior art -- say which

kill_condition: Primary evaluations in low- and middle-income countries (randomised or credible quasi-experimental studies) consistently show that specific programme types improve both enrolment or attendance and measured learning for children with disabilities, with effects large enough to matter. Systematic reviews also rate certainty in those effects as moderate or high. In that case the common belief is simply confirmed and there is no story.

kill_condition_tested._note: Filled in AFTER going to look, by whoever looked.

scope._note: What the answer will and will not cover, written at step 1 BEFORE any source is opened, so scope cannot be fitted to the findings afterwards. An omission ruled OUT_OF_SCOPE, and a headline conclusion declared out of scope, must name the question's words or one of these entries (fix 2, docs/whu-fix2-omission-rulings-design.md section 2.4).
scope.covers: Interventions intended to improve educational access, participation, retention or learning outcomes for children and young people with disabilities (any impairment type, roughly ages 3–24) in low- and middle-income countries. It covers how effective they are, how the effects compare across programme types, and how much confidence the evidence supports.

out.what: Effectiveness of disability-inclusive education in high-income countries
out.why: Different school systems, resources and baseline services make the findings non-transferable, and the question specifies low- and middle-income countries.

out.what: Whether inclusive or segregated schooling is the right approach as a matter of rights
out.why: That is a normative and legal question (e.g. under international disability rights commitments), not an empirical question about effectiveness.

out.what: How many children with disabilities are out of school, and how disability should be measured
out.why: Prevalence and measurement are context for the question, not evidence about whether programmes work.

out.what: Health, rehabilitation or functional outcomes not tied to education
out.why: The question is about educational outcomes. Clinical or functional gains are only relevant where they are measured alongside schooling outcomes.

out.what: General education quality interventions not targeted at, or not reporting results for, children with disabilities
out.why: Without disaggregated results, they say nothing about this population.

evidence_standard._note: What kinds of evidence the answer will weigh, written at step 1 BEFORE any source is opened (post-study fix 3, docs/whu-fix3-evidence-standard.md). 'measured': outcomes measured in trials, cohorts, evaluations. 'assessed': expert assessments -- systematic-review conclusions, IPCC confidence-rated statements, guideline recommendations. When they differ, the page states both and drops neither.
evidence_standard.measured: Effect estimates from primary studies with a comparison group (RCTs, difference-in-differences, matched or regression-discontinuity designs) on outcomes for children with disabilities in low- and middle-income countries. Outcomes include enrolment, attendance, retention or dropout, progression, and test-based learning (literacy, numeracy). Sample sizes, impairment types, follow-up length, and whether learning, not just access, was measured are all part of this evidence.
evidence_standard.assessed: Certainty or confidence ratings that systematic reviews, evidence gap maps or expert panels assign to bodies of evidence for each intervention type, such as GRADE-style ratings or risk-of-bias judgements, along with their conclusions about which programme types have sufficient versus insufficient evidence.
